topic: CORS is enforced by browsers: it doesn't stop requests reaching your API
text:
"We have CORS configured, so other sites can't call our API." That's a dangerous assumption.

Per MDN, browsers enforce CORS, not servers. It decides whether a page's JavaScript may read a cross-origin response.

It doesn't stop the request from being sent. MDN notes a server doesn't have to opt in to receive any request that looks like a form submission: GET, HEAD, or POST with a form-style content type skip the preflight.

So a cross-site page can still fire that POST. curl, Postman and scripts ignore CORS entirely.

What actually protects an endpoint:
• Authenticate and authorize every request on the server
• Use CSRF protection (tokens or SameSite cookies) for cookie-based sessions
• Treat CORS as a relaxing rule for browsers, not a lock

My rule of thumb: if the endpoint would be unsafe with CORS turned off, it's already unsafe.

Have you ever seen a "fixed" CORS error cause a security gap, like Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * on an authenticated API?
